summary.text: Sexual selection is a mechanism of evolution in which members of one sex choose mates and members of the same sex compete for access to the other sex.
It means some individuals have greater reproductive success than others, for example because they are more attractive.
It can push males to extreme displays, producing differences between the sexes such as the ornate plumage of peafowl or the antlers of deer.

facts.label: Wallace's view
facts.value: A relatively weak form of selection

facts.label: Fisherian runaway
facts.value: Positive feedback between a trait and the preference for it

facts.label: Flour beetle study
facts.value: Sexual selection protected an inbred population against extinction

items.prompt: In one species, males battle each other over mating access. In another, females pick among displaying males. What do these patterns show?

options.label: Two unrelated processes, neither a form of selection
Two names for a single form of competition
One form acting on males and another only on offspring
The two forms: competition within a sex and mate choice by the other

items.explain: Sexual selection combines choice of mates by one sex (intersexual) with competition within a sex for access to the other (intrasexual).

items.prompt: A male loses every contest for mates but lives a long life. In evolutionary terms, what has his loss cost him?

options.label: His life, since losers in these contests die
Offspring, since losing means few or no young
His strength, which fades with each defeat
His genes, which are erased from the population

items.explain: In sexual selection, the result is not death to the unsuccessful competitor, but few or no offspring.

items.prompt: In a species, females increasingly favour a showier male trait, and the trait keeps getting showier. Why can this escalate rather than settle?

options.label: A feedback loop links the trait in one sex to the preference in the other
Males grow stronger each generation and so win more fights
Females want fewer offspring and so choose more carefully
Natural selection always rewards the showiest trait

items.explain: Passing on the desire for a trait in one sex is as important as having the trait in the other, creating a positive feedback loop that produces extravagant structures.

items.prompt: A female widowbird picks the male with the longest tail. How does that choice help her genes spread?

options.label: Long tails help males find food for her chicks
Long tails help her offspring survive the winter
Her sons will attract later females and father many offspring with her genes
Long tails make her own eggs more numerous

items.explain: She mates with the most attractive long-tailed male so that her sons will themselves be attractive to the next generation's females, fathering many offspring that carry her genes.

items.prompt: A bright ornament does not help its owner survive, yet it persists. What does Darwin's idea of sexual selection suggest?

options.label: It must secretly help the owner survive, or it would vanish
It can persist by winning mates or beating rivals, without aiding survival
It persists by chance alone, with no link to reproduction
It persists only because humans prefer to breed it

items.explain: Darwin felt natural selection alone could not account for certain non-survival adaptations, and he divided sexual selection into male-male competition and female choice.

items.prompt: A ten-year lab experiment changed only how strongly mate competition acted on flour beetle populations. What did it find about inbred groups?

options.label: Sexual selection protected even an inbred population against extinction
Sexual selection made inbred groups die out faster
Sexual selection had no effect on inbred groups
Sexual selection protected only populations that were not inbred

items.explain: A ten-year study that varied sexual selection on flour beetles with other factors held constant showed it protected even an inbred population against extinction.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing and competing
paragraphs.text: Sexual selection is one of the ways evolution works. It has two sides. Members of one sex pick partners from the other sex, which is called intersexual selection, and members of the same sex compete for access to the other sex, which is called intrasexual selection. Both mean that some individuals in a population leave more offspring than others, perhaps because they are better looking, or because they favour better-looking partners.

paragraphs.heading: Why the sexes differ
paragraphs.text: Successful males gain by mating often and by keeping one or more fertile females to themselves. Females get the most out of the energy they spend on reproduction by choosing the best males. This can drive males to great lengths to show they are fit to be chosen, which produces sexual dimorphism: clear differences between the sexes, such as the showy feathers of peafowl and birds-of-paradise or the antlers of deer. In some species these roles are reversed. Sexual selection is common across the animal kingdom and also turns up in plants and fungi.

paragraphs.heading: Darwin and his critics
paragraphs.text: Charles Darwin first proposed the idea in On the Origin of Species in 1859 and developed it in The Descent of Man in 1871. He felt natural selection by itself could not explain some features that do not help an animal survive. He split sexual selection into competition between males and choice by females. Alfred Russel Wallace partly opposed him, mostly after Darwin died. Wallace accepted that sexual selection happened but thought it weak, and he doubted that animals such as beetles could judge beauty.

paragraphs.heading: The runaway loop
paragraphs.text: The statistician and biologist Ronald Fisher built on Darwin's ideas in The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection, a book he published in 1930. He saw that a female's liking for a feature can be passed on genetically together with the genes for the feature itself. Offspring of both sexes inherit both sets of genes. This sets up a loop that feeds itself, called a Fisherian runaway, in which the feature and the taste for it grow together until physical limits stop them.

paragraphs.heading: The long-tailed widowbird
paragraphs.text: The long-tailed widowbird is a classic case. Males grow long tails because females choose them for it, and female taste goes further still: females are drawn to tails longer than any that occur in nature. A female picks the male with the most appealing long tail so that her sons may be attractive to the next generation of females. Those sons can then father many young that carry her genes.

paragraphs.heading: From side issue to major force
paragraphs.text: Biologists did not treat the idea as very important until the 1930s, when they began counting it as a form of natural selection. Even then many leading theorists gave it little attention, and Fisher was the main exception. Only in the 1960s and 1970s, through Robert Trivers and others, did biology come to see it as one of the major drivers of evolution. In the 1990s Marion Petrie showed that peahens chose males with showier plumage. A ten-year study of flour beetles found that sexual selection protected even an inbred population from dying out.
